title: Starting in 2027, AI and Search Services for K-12 Student Accounts Will Be Disabled by Default; Disabling AI Will Also Remove Traditional Search

content_html:
On November 3 local time, Google officially announced that it will make major changes starting in 2027 to its AI feature management policy for K-12 (kindergarten through high school) education users. Under the new rules, for school-managed K-12 student accounts, related services such as Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search will all be set to off by default, and can only be used normally after a school administrator actively authorizes them.

Giving Schools Control, but an All-or-Nothing Linkage Sparks New Debate

Google said the adjustment was decided after full communication with schools, teachers, researchers, and policymakers, with the core aim of allowing schools to decide for themselves, based on their own needs, how AI tools are used in classroom teaching.

However, the new policy also comes with a controversial bundled restriction: if a school chooses to completely disable AI, students will also no longer be able to use traditional Google Search. In an interview, Chris Phillips, Vice President and General Manager of Google's Education business, pointed out that because search and AI are now deeply integrated, schools currently cannot separately turn off features such as AI Overview in Google Search while keeping traditional web search service.

This means that for educational institutions that want students to continue using search engines to find information and compare sources, but do not yet want them to access generative AI features, they will face a difficult all-or-nothing trade-off in the future. If a school chooses to completely disable AI features, students trying to use search services will only see a disabled notice provided by the school.

Introducing Guided Learning to Support Learning and Respond to Outside Concerns

Alongside this policy adjustment, Google is also gradually advancing positive guidance tools for educational settings. Among them, Guided Learning, which aims to guide students to understand problems on their own through questioning, step-by-step explanations, and interactive exercises (rather than directly providing answers), has been announced for introduction into Google Classroom and is planned to later be integrated into Google Search for student accounts.

According to the official plan, Guided Learning will first be piloted in some schools in the United States, and coverage will gradually expand after widely collecting practical feedback from frontline teachers. Google hopes that through such features, AI can truly play the role of a learning-assistance tool in the classroom.

Previously, many educational institutions and parents expressed deep concern about the potential impact AI tools could have on students' independent thinking ability, how they complete daily homework, and the learning process. By setting the relevant tools to off by default, Google has returned the choice to schools, but the deep integration of search services and AI features has still sparked a new discussion in the education world about the boundaries of technology and the trade-offs of its use.
